items.title: 0.6 Dashboards served
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: –
  • Records: DD-017, DD-019, DD-034 (supersedes DD-018), DD-035; relies on DD-001, ADR 046

items.title: Scope
items.text:
The two Apache Atlas 2.4.0 user interfaces are served where Atlas serves them — dashboardv2 at / and dashboardv3 at /n/ — by the dashboard image, an nginx container that keeps the API on the same origin by proxying /api/ to the Aurelius Atlas server (DD-001).

  • apps/aurelius-atlas-dashboard: the dashboardv2 and dashboardv3 source of the release-2.4.0 tag, vendored unchanged apart from the patches listed in its PATCHES.md, with a build target that compiles both in a hardened Node container, and an nginx image that serves the built files and proxies /api/, dashboardv3's /n directory redirect and the login root j_spring_security_check to the server (DD-034).
  • aurelius-atlas-server: serves the API only; its image no longer contains the dashboards.
  • Proof: the end-to-end tests load both dashboards in a browser against the dashboard image, with the server's API behind its proxy.

Not in scope:

Not delivered here Delivered by The data the dashboards show (types, entities, search, lineage, …) 1.x to 5.x The login page (login.jsp) and the redirect to it 6.1 Changes to the dashboards' behaviour or look not planned (ADR 046, DD-001)

Until those increments land, the dashboards load and show errors for every call the server does not answer yet. That is the expected state, not a deviation.

items.title: Semantics
items.text:
Id Rule DSH-01 GET / answers the built dashboardv2 index.html, and every other built dashboardv2 file is served at its path below / DSH-02 GET /n/ answers the built dashboardv3 index.html, and every other built dashboardv3 file is served at its path below /n/; /n redirects to /n/ DSH-03 The API takes precedence: a path the API answers is never served from the dashboards, and a path neither answers is 404 DSH-04 The server serves the API only: on its own origin, no dashboard path answers DSH-05 The dashboards are built from the vendored release-2.4.0 source, changed only by the patches in apps/aurelius-atlas-dashboard/PATCHES.md DSH-06 In a browser, each dashboard loads from the dashboard image and asks it for /api/atlas/admin/session, which answers 200 DSH-10 The proxy forwards the origin's Host, port included, so an upstream-generated absolute redirect (FastAPI's slash normalization) keeps the public origin

DSH-05 keeps the dashboards those of Atlas 2.4.0: the vendored source is byte-identical to the tag and every change is one reviewed patch (DD-017). DSH-01 to DSH-04 serve them on one origin that also answers the API, as Atlas does (DD-034): the dashboard image serves the files and proxies /api/ to the server, whose routes keep the prefix. DSH-03's precedence is nginx's longest-prefix match: /api/ reaches the server even where a dashboard file has the same name.

items.title: Java origin
items.text:
Apache Atlas release-2.4.0:

  • dashboardv2/, dashboardv3/: the user interfaces, vendored
  • webapp/pom.xml, dashboardv2/pom.xml, dashboardv3/pom.xml: where the builds go in the web application (dashboardv2 at the root, dashboardv3 under n/) and the grunt build-minify step
  • Atlas's web application is a servlet container serving both dashboards and the API from one origin; the dashboard image keeps that shape with a proxy instead of a shared process (DD-034)

items.title: Deviations
items.text: DV-09: serving the dashboards from nginx instead of the API's process changes what a browser observes around the dashboards — /n answers 308 where the serving process directory-redirected, hardening headers are added, and the origin speaks TLS per container. None that a client of the REST API sees. The dashboards' stylesheets are compiled by dart-sass instead of libsass (DD-017); the JavaScript is identical to Atlas's build.

items.title: Acceptance
items.text:
• apps/aurelius-atlas-dashboard/ — PATCHES.md and the build (DSH-05), run by nx build aurelius-atlas-dashboard and by the dashboard image's build.
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-dashboard/ — its stack (docker-compose.yaml) runs the dashboard image and the API-only server on the dev store, and its e2e/ tests prove both dashboards, the /n redirect, the proxy's precedence, the forwarded Host and the server's API-only origin (DSH-01 to DSH-04, DSH-10) against it, plus both dashboards in Chromium against the dashboard image (DSH-05, DSH-06).

items.title: 1.1 Typedef models
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: –
  • Records: DD-020, DD-021, DD-022; relies on DD-002, DD-013, ADR 046

items.title: Scope
items.text:
The data shapes of Atlas type definitions, in a new library without I/O, libs/python/aurelius-atlas-model (package aurelius_atlas_model, DD-002):

  • the six type definitions: enum, struct, classification, entity, relationship and business metadata, with their parts (attribute, constraint, enum element, relationship end and relationship attribute definitions);
  • the type definition header and AtlasTypesDef, the body of /v2/types/typedefs;
  • reading them from and writing them to the JSON Atlas uses on its REST API, and the small helpers the Java classes offer (attribute and element lookup, super types, built-in type names).

No endpoint changes; the server does not use the library yet.

Not in scope:

Not delivered here Delivered by Resolving type names, supertypes and constraints; validation errors 1.2 Defaults the type registry fills in (relationship category, tags, …) 1.3 Storing type definitions; the built-in models at start-up 1.4, 1.5 /v2/types/...; malformed bodies answered with Atlas's error and 400 1.6 Order-insensitive comparison of set-valued arrays in parity scenarios 1.6 (DD-013) The paged lists (AtlasStructDefs, … built on PList) 1.6

items.title: Semantics
items.text:
"Reading" is what Atlas's Jackson mapper does with a REST request body; "writing" is what it puts in a response. Atlas serialises the models with Jackson 2.12 (AtlasJsonProvider, no date or naming customisation) and the annotations on each class (DD-020).

Id Rule TDM-01 Every field is read and written under the name of its Java getter: isOptional, valuesMinCount, includeInNotification, endDef1, relationshipAttributeDefs, businessAttributeDefs, … TDM-02 Writing leaves out a field whose value is null; an empty list, set or map is written TDM-03 Reading ignores fields the model does not have TDM-04 Each type definition writes its category (ENUM, STRUCT, CLASSIFICATION, ENTITY, RELATIONSHIP, BUSINESS_METADATA), fixed by its kind; a category in the input is ignored. The header reads and writes category like any field TDM-05 createTime and updateTime are written as milliseconds since the epoch, and read from such a number or from an ISO-8601 date-time string (DD-022) TDM-06 attributeDefs (struct and its kinds), elementDefs (enum), superTypes (classification, entity) and entityTypes (classification) are never null: missing, null or empty reads as empty TDM-07 Of attribute definitions with the same name, compared without case, only the last is kept, at its own position; an attribute definition without a name is dropped TDM-08 Of enum elements with the same value, compared without case, only the last is kept, at its own position; an element without a value is dropped TDM-09 superTypes, subTypes and entityTypes hold each name once (DD-021) TDM-10 An attribute definition without them reads as isOptional false, cardinality SINGLE, valuesMinCount and valuesMaxCount -1, isUnique, isIndexable and includeInNotification false, searchWeight -1; an explicit null reads as false or 0, as in Java TDM-11 An empty constraints list reads as null and is not written; options maps are copied TDM-12 A relationship end without them reads as cardinality SINGLE, isContainer and isLegacyAttribute false; a relationship definition keeps relationshipCategory, propagateTags and its ends null when they are not given TDM-13 AtlasTypesDef reads each of its six lists as empty when missing and keeps an explicit null, which it does not write TDM-14 Type categories, cardinalities, index types, relationship categories and tag propagations are read and written by their Java names, with case; any other value is rejected TDM-15 Scalars are coerced as Jackson 2.12 coerces them by default: a number into a string field, a numeric or boolean string into a number or boolean field. A value that cannot be coerced, such as an object where a string is expected, is rejected with an error that names the field TDM-16 Attribute definitions and enum elements are found, replaced and removed by name or value without case; super types and entity types by exact name. Options and constraint parameters are read and set by exact key, a constraint's type is compared without case, and the isSoftReference and isAppendOnPartialUpdate options are true only for the value true, without case TDM-17 AtlasTypesDef is empty when all six lists are empty or null, and tells whether it holds a type definition of a kind by exact name TDM-18 A header made from a type definition carries its guid, name, category and serviceType TDM-19 array<T> and map<K,V> type names are built as Atlas builds them, and the primitive, built-in and relationship attribute type names are Atlas's TDM-20 Writing a model and reading the result gives an equal model; the type definitions of Atlas's 0010-base_model.json and 0011-glossary_model.json read without error

TDM-06 to TDM-13 are the Java setters' and constructors' normalisations, which run when Jackson reads a body: a client that sends a duplicate attribute or no cardinality sees the normalised definition in the response.

items.text:
Apache Atlas release-2.4.0, intg/src/main/java/org/apache/atlas/model/:

  • typedef/AtlasBaseTypeDef, AtlasStructDef (with AtlasAttributeDef, AtlasConstraintDef), AtlasEnumDef (with AtlasEnumElementDef), AtlasClassificationDef, AtlasEntityDef (with AtlasRelationshipAttributeDef), AtlasRelationshipDef, AtlasRelationshipEndDef, AtlasBusinessMetadataDef, AtlasTypeDefHeader, AtlasTypesDef
  • TypeCategory
  • webapp/.../web/util/AtlasJsonProvider: the REST mapper (Jackson defaults, big decimals for floats)
  • tests: intg/src/test/java/org/apache/atlas/model/typedef/TestAtlas*Def.java

items.text: None. Java writes sets in HashSet order, which Atlas does not define; parity scenarios will compare those arrays without order (DD-013, from 1.6).

items.title: Acceptance
items.text:

  • uv run aurelius-atlas-trace check — every public function and rule is named by a test.

items.title: 1.2 Type registry
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: –
  • Records: DD-023, DD-024, DD-025; relies on DD-002, DD-020

items.title: Scope
items.text:
The registry that turns type definitions into resolved types, in a new library without I/O, libs/python/aurelius-atlas-typesystem (package aurelius_atlas_typesystem, DD-002):

  • the registry: the built-in types, lookup by name and GUID, the definitions per kind, and updates made on a transient copy that is committed or discarded;
  • the types: built-in, array, map, enum and struct, and for classification, entity, relationship and business metadata definitions their own attributes, resolved as a struct's are;
  • attribute resolution: attribute types, cardinality, the classification and business metadata ban, and the ownedRef and inverseRef constraints;
  • the Atlas error codes these raise, in the model library, where every layer can raise them (DD-023).

No endpoint changes; the server does not use the registry yet.

Not in scope:

Not delivered here Delivered by Super and sub types, inherited attributes, root types, classification entityTypes 1.3 Relationship ends and relationship attributes; business metadata applicableEntityTypes 1.3 Rejecting duplicate or reserved type names, and type names already in use 1.4 (the store) Validating, normalising and defaulting attribute values 2.1 (DD-025) JanusGraph property names, index field names and index-query escaping dropped (DD-025)

items.title: Semantics
items.text:
Id Rule TRG-01 A new registry holds the built-in types boolean, byte, short, int, long, float, double, biginteger, bigdecimal, date and string (category PRIMITIVE) and objectid (OBJECT_ID_TYPE), all with service type atlas_core TRG-02 A registered name answers its type. An unregistered array<T> or map<K,V> name is built on demand from its element, key and value types, splitting a map's at its first comma; an array built so has cardinality LIST and no element counts TRG-03 An unknown type name fails with TYPE_NAME_NOT_FOUND (404) and an unknown GUID with TYPE_GUID_NOT_FOUND (404), each naming what was asked for TRG-04 Definitions are found by name and by GUID, per kind and across all kinds; each kind lists its definitions, names and types, and the registry lists all type names, all types and all service types TRG-05 The registry changes only through a transient copy taken under the update lock. Committing makes the copy's types the registry's; releasing without committing discards them. The lock is re-entrant; waiting longer than its timeout fails with FAILED_TO_OBTAIN_TYPE_UPDATE_LOCK (500) (DD-024) TRG-06 Adding a definition registers it by name and, when it has one, by GUID. A later definition with the same name replaces the earlier one, a built-in type included TRG-07 Updating replaces the definition with the given GUID or name; a definition updated without a target is found by its GUID, else by its name, else ignored TRG-08 Removing by GUID or by name removes the definition under both. Removing the definitions of an AtlasTypesDef removes each by its GUID when it has one, else by its name. The transient copy records what was added, updated and removed, in order TRG-09 After every change the copy resolves every type again; the first failure is raised and nothing reaches the registry TRG-10 Each attribute's type must resolve. LIST and SET cardinality need an array type, else INVALID_ATTRIBUTE_TYPE_FOR_CARDINALITY (400); the array then takes the attribute's cardinality and value counts. An attribute whose type, array element or map value is a classification or business metadata type fails with ATTRIBUTE_TYPE_INVALID (400) TRG-11 An attribute's qualified name is Type.attribute, or its name when that contains a dot. An entity type in an attribute becomes objectid of that entity type, also inside arrays and maps; such an array or map is a new one, so an array keeps cardinality LIST and no value counts, as in Java. The attribute is an object reference when its type, array element or map value is objectid TRG-12 ownedRef needs an entity type (or an array or map of one), else CONSTRAINT_OWNED_REF_ATTRIBUTE_INVALID_TYPE. inverseRef needs one too (CONSTRAINT_INVERSE_REF_ATTRIBUTE_INVALID_TYPE), a non-blank attribute parameter (CONSTRAINT_MISSING_PARAMS), that attribute defined on the referenced entity type (CONSTRAINT_INVERSE_REF_INVERSE_ATTRIBUTE_NON_EXISTING) and of an entity type (CONSTRAINT_INVERSE_REF_INVERSE_ATTRIBUTE_INVALID_TYPE), all 400; the inverse attribute is then linked TRG-13 A type's attributes are looked up by exact name; its unique attributes are those whose definition is unique TRG-14 An enum type finds its elements by value without case and by ordinal; its default is the definition's defaultValue, else the first element's value TRG-15 Every error carries Atlas's HTTP status, error code and message, with {0}, {1}, … filled in from its parameters in order TRG-16 Classification, entity, relationship and business metadata types resolve their own attributes as a struct type does

TRG-06 to TRG-08 copy the registry's own behaviour: it accepts what it is given. The checks that a name is new, not reserved and not in use are the type definition store's (AtlasTypeDefGraphStore), ported in 1.4.

items.title: Java origin
items.text:
Apache Atlas release-2.4.0, intg/src/main/java/org/apache/atlas/:

  • type/AtlasTypeRegistry (with AtlasTransientTypeRegistry, TypeRegistryUpdateSynchronizer, TypeCache, TypeDefCache), AtlasType, AtlasBuiltInTypes, AtlasArrayType, AtlasMapType, AtlasEnumType, AtlasStructType (with AtlasAttribute): the definition side only (DD-025)
  • AtlasErrorCode, exception/AtlasBaseException
  • tests: intg/src/test/java/org/apache/atlas/type/TestAtlasTypeRegistry.java, TestAtlasStructType.java, TestAtlasArrayType.java, TestAtlasMapType.java, TestAtlasEnumType.java

items.title: Acceptance

  • libs/python/aurelius-atlas-model/tests/ — the error codes and messages (TRG-15).

items.title: 1.3 Type hierarchies
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: –
  • Records: DD-026, DD-027; relies on DD-021, DD-024, DD-025

items.title: Scope
items.text:
The parts of the type system that link types to each other, in aurelius-atlas-typesystem:

  • entity and classification hierarchies: super types, all super and sub types, inherited attributes, the root types with the system attributes, and the sub types written back to the definitions;
  • the entity type's derived attributes: header and minimal-info attributes, the display-text attribute, owned references and whether the type is internal;
  • the entity types a classification may be applied to;
  • relationship types: their ends, label and the relationship attributes they add to entity types, which are inherited and written back to the entity definitions with the tag-propagation edges;
  • business metadata types: their attributes, the entity types they apply to, and the business attributes written back to the entity definitions;
  • Atlas error messages formatted as Java's MessageFormat formats them.

No endpoint changes.

Not in scope:

Not delivered here Delivered by Dynamic attributes (dynAttribute: templates) and their evaluation order 2.4 (DD-026) The root entity type's lookup of business attributes for search 4.1 (DD-026) Logging relationship definitions an entity attribute lacks (reportMissingRelationshipDef) not ported Index-query strings of type names (getTypeAndAllSubTypesQryStr) dropped (DD-025)

items.title: Semantics
items.text:
Id Rule THY-01 An entity type's super types must be entity types and a classification's must be classifications, else INCOMPATIBLE_SUPERTYPE (400) with the super type's name first and the type's second, as Java passes them THY-02 A type that reaches itself through its super types fails with CIRCULAR_REFERENCE (400), naming the type and the types visited on the way, as [A, B] THY-03 A type's attributes are those of all its super types, depth first in the order the super types are given, then its own. A name defined by two different types of the hierarchy fails with ATTRIBUTE_NAME_ALREADY_EXISTS_IN_ANOTHER_PARENT_TYPE (400); a super type reached twice is not a conflict THY-04 Each type knows its super types, all super types and the sub types and all sub types that every other type's super types give it, each also with the type itself. Sub types are written to the definition's subTypes THY-05 __ENTITY_ROOT and __CLASSIFICATION_ROOT hold Atlas's system attributes (__guid, __typeName, __timestamp, …); every entity and classification type finds them by name after its own and inherited attributes. Root types are not registered, and their attribute names are not qualified THY-06 An entity type's header attributes are its unique attributes and name, description, owner and createTime; its minimal-info attributes add those its schemaAttributes option lists. Its display-text attribute is its displayTextAttribute option, else a direct super type's option, else any super type's, when that names an attribute. It is internal when __internal is among its super types. Its owned references are the attributes and relationship attributes with ownedRef THY-07 A classification applies to its entityTypes and all their sub types (an unknown name fails with TYPE_NAME_NOT_FOUND), narrowed by what its super types allow. Super types whose allowed types do not overlap fail with CLASSIFICATIONDEF_PARENTS_ENTITYTYPES_DISJOINT, and own types outside them with CLASSIFICATIONDEF_ENTITYTYPES_NOT_PARENTS_SUBSET (400); with no own types it applies where its super types allow; with no restriction anywhere, to every entity type THY-08 A relationship's two ends need a type (MISSING_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE, endDef1.type) that is an entity type (RELATIONSHIPDEF_INVALID_END_TYPE) and a name. No end may be LIST; not both ends may be containers; a container needs AGGREGATION or COMPOSITION, which in turn need a container; a COMPOSITION end with SET must be the container. Each breach has its Atlas code (400) THY-09 A relationship's label is its relationshipLabel, else r: and its name when neither end is a legacy attribute, else __ and the qualified name of the legacy end's attribute THY-10 Each end adds a relationship attribute named after the end to its entity type. When the type has no attribute of that name, the attribute is new: it holds the other end's type (array<…> for SET), with the end's cardinality, optional except on a composition's child end, and ownedRef on a composition's container end. Otherwise the existing attribute is used and marked legacy. Each has the relationship's name, edge label and an edge direction (OUT, IN or BOTH) THY-11 Sub types inherit relationship attributes; the first a type gets per attribute and relationship stays. They are written to the entity definition's relationshipAttributeDefs with their relationship's name and legacy flag, and with isAppendOnPartialUpdate when the type's appendRelationshipsOnPartialUpdate option lists them. A relationship's label is the type's tag-propagation edge when its propagateTags sends classifications from that type THY-12 A business metadata attribute may not hold a struct, classification or business metadata type, nor an array or map of one (BUSINESS_METADATA_DEF_ATTRIBUTE_TYPE_INVALID); its applicableEntityTypes option must name entity types; a string attribute needs a maxStrLength option (MISSING_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE). Business attributes are added to the entity types they apply to and their sub types, found as bm.attribute, and written to the entity definition's businessAttributeDefs THY-13 Error messages follow MessageFormat: an apostrophe starts or ends quoted text, which is copied as is and loses the apostrophe, and two apostrophes are one; collection parameters are written as [a, b]

THY-04, THY-11 and THY-12 change the definitions the registry holds, as Java does. The definitions Types REST returns (1.6) therefore carry subTypes, relationshipAttributeDefs and businessAttributeDefs.

items.title: 1.4 Typedef store
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: –
  • Records: DD-028, DD-029, DD-030, DV-06; relies on ADR 047, DD-002, DD-005, DD-024

items.title: Scope
items.text:
Type definitions are kept in Elasticsearch and loaded into the type registry when the server starts, in a new library libs/python/aurelius-atlas-core (package aurelius_atlas_core, the -core layer of DD-002):

  • the typedef store: create, update and delete type definitions, with the checks Atlas's store makes and its registry does not (unique and well-formed names, no attribute removed, no type deleted while something refers to it), and the audit fields;
  • the stored form: what Atlas keeps of a definition, which is what it answers with afterwards;
  • persistence in one Elasticsearch document, written with optimistic concurrency (DD-028, DD-029);
  • the server loads the stored definitions into its registry at start-up and keeps it in step with other processes.

No endpoint changes: /v2/types arrives in 1.6.

Not in scope:

Not delivered here Delivered by Atlas's built-in models (addons/models), the model patches and createUpdate 1.5 /v2/types/..., search filters over type definitions, authorization of type reads 1.6, 6.2 Refusing to delete a type that entities or classifications still use 2.2 (DD-030) Attribute names that are DSL keywords (atlas.types.allowReservedKeywords) not ported (*)

(*) Atlas allows them by default; the check is off unless that setting is changed.

items.title: Semantics
items.text: Id Rule TDS-01 Creating definitions resolves them with every stored type first (TRG-09); an unknown type name or GUID found then fails with BAD_REQUEST (400) carrying the resolution's message. Nothing is stored unless every definition passes TDS-02 A definition's name must match [a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_ ]*, optionally prefixed with __, else TYPE_NAME_INVALID_FORMAT (400); a name already stored fails with TYPE_ALREADY_EXISTS (409), and a name another kind holds with TYPE_MATCH_FAILED (400), naming Atlas's legacy kind (CLASS, TRAIT, STRUCT, …) TDS-03 A created definition gets typeVersion 1.0, version 1, a random GUID and the current time as createTime and updateTime, each only when it has none; its description defaults to its name; createdBy and updatedBy are the current user (none until 6.1, DV-06) TDS-04 Every attribute must have a name and a type name (MISSING_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE); a type it names that is neither built in nor stored fails with UNKNOWN_TYPE (400). A struct needs attributes (BAD_REQUEST, Missing attributes for structdef); a business metadata attribute's name must match the type name pattern (ATTRIBUTE_NAME_INVALID_CHARS). An enum needs elements, and each element a value and an ordinal (MISSING_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE, values and elementValue) TDS-05 An attribute is stored in Atlas's form and read back from it: cardinality and counts become isOptional, valuesMinCount and valuesMaxCount as Atlas's multiplicity gives them (an optional single value reads 0 and 1, an unbounded list or set 2147483647); only ownedRef and inverseRef constraints are kept, in that order; options, default value, description, display name, search weight and index type are kept TDS-06 A stored relationship without a category is ASSOCIATION, and without propagateTags is NONE; its label and ends are kept as given TDS-07 Updating finds each definition by its GUID when it has one, else by its name (TYPE_GUID_NOT_FOUND or TYPE_NAME_NOT_FOUND, 404, mapped to BAD_REQUEST while resolving, as TDS-01). The name, the kind and the creation fields stay; blank fields keep their stored value; version goes up by one and updateTime and updatedBy are set TDS-08 An update may not remove an attribute (ATTRIBUTE_DELETION_NOT_SUPPORTED), change an attribute's type (BAD_REQUEST, Data type update for attribute is not supported) or add a mandatory one (CANNOT_ADD_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE); a relationship's name, category and ends may not change (RELATIONSHIPDEF_INVALID_*_UPDATE, with Java's text of the ends); a business metadata attribute may not lose applicable entity types (APPLICABLE_ENTITY_TYPES_DELETION_NOT_SUPPORTED); super types may not be removed (SUPERTYPE_REMOVAL_NOT_SUPPORTED), nor some of a classification's entity types (ENTITYTYPE_REMOVAL_NOT_SUPPORTED), though all of them may. A classification's entity types must be stored entity types, on create too (CLASSIFICATIONDEF_INVALID_ENTITYTYPES) TDS-09 Deleting finds each definition by GUID, else name, and fails with TYPE_HAS_REFERENCES (409) while another stored type refers to it as a super type, an attribute type or a classification's entity type, and an entity type with TYPE_HAS_RELATIONSHIPS (409) while a relationship ends on it. References from definitions deleted in the same request do not count, so a relationship and the types it ends on may be deleted together TDS-10 A change is written only after the transient registry resolved it, then committed to the registry; when the write fails, nothing is committed and the stored document is unchanged TDS-11 The stored definitions are one document whose Elasticsearch version guards every write: a write based on an older version fails, the process reloads and the change is retried once, else FAILED_TO_OBTAIN_TYPE_UPDATE_LOCK (500) (DD-028, DD-029) TDS-12 At start-up the server loads the stored definitions into its registry, dropping a second definition with the same name and an ownedRef constraint on an attribute that refers to no entity type, as Atlas's rectifyTypeErrorsIfAny does; with nothing stored, the registry holds the built-in types only TDS-13 A process whose registry is older than the stored document reloads it before it changes types, and at least every AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_TYPEDEF_REFRESH_SECONDS (default 5) before it answers

items.title: 1.5 Built-in models and patches
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: –
  • Records: DD-031, DD-032, DD-033, DV-07, DV-08; relies on DD-028, DD-029, DV-06

items.title: Scope
items.text:
When the server starts, it loads Atlas's built-in type definitions (addons/models) and their patches into the typedef store of 1.4, as AtlasTypeDefStoreInitializer does:

  • the 2.4.0 models, vendored unchanged into aurelius-atlas-core (DD-032), read from a directory the server can be pointed at (AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_MODELS_DIR);
  • each model file creates the types not yet stored and updates those whose typeVersion is newer (createUpdateTypesDef);
  • the typedef patches, with the nine patch actions of Atlas 2.4.0, and the record of each patch's outcome, kept in the typedef document (DD-031);
  • processes that start together apply each file and each patch once (DD-033).

No endpoint changes: the loaded types are served by /v2/types in 1.6.

Not in scope:

Not delivered here Delivered by /v2/types/... 1.6 admin/patches, and the Java patches (AtlasPatchManager, UniqueAttributePatch, …) 2.2 Setting the default of a new mandatory attribute, and new super types, on existing entities 2.2 Deferring the load until an instance becomes active (atlas.server.ha.enabled) not ported The legacy TypesResource (/api/atlas/types), the other caller of createUpdateTypesDef not ported

AddMandatoryAttributesPatch and SuperTypesUpdatePatch, which ADD_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE and ADD_SUPER_TYPES schedule, change entities; without entities there is nothing for them to do until 2.2. High availability is replaced by DD-029 and DD-033: every process may load the models.

items.title: Semantics
items.text: Id Rule MDL-01 The models directory is read in name order: each sub-directory except one named patches, then the directory itself. Of each, the files are loaded in name order, then the files of its patches sub-directory are applied in name order. Other entries are ignored; a missing directory loads nothing. Names compare as Java's String.compareTo MDL-02 A model file is an AtlasTypesDef; an empty one is skipped. Its definitions whose name is not registered, as any kind or built-in, are created. A definition whose name is registered as the same kind is updated when its typeVersion is greater than the registered one, compared as strings with an absent version less than any; the update keeps the registered attributes it lacks, appended in order, and an enum the registered elements it lacks MDL-03 A file's creations and updates are one change (createUpdateTypesDef): the updates replace the registered definitions without resolving, the creations are then resolved (an unknown type name fails with BAD_REQUEST, as TDS-01) and stored with TDS-02 to TDS-06, then the updates are stored with TDS-07 and TDS-08. Nothing of the file is stored unless all of it passes MDL-04 A model file that cannot be read, is not an AtlasTypesDef or fails MDL-03 is logged and skipped; loading goes on with the next file MDL-05 A patch file holds patches, a list of patches with id, description, action, typeName, applyToVersion, updateToVersion, params, attributeDefs, elementDefs, typeDefOptions, serviceType, attributeName and superTypes; other fields are ignored. A patch whose action is not one of the nine is logged and skipped. A patch whose id is recorded APPLIED or SKIPPED is not applied again; one recorded FAILED or UNKNOWN, or not recorded, is. A patch without an id is applied at every start and not recorded (DV-08) MDL-06 A patch ends APPLIED, SKIPPED or UNKNOWN as its action decides, or FAILED when it raises an Atlas error; its record (id, description, type TYPEDEF_PATCH, action, status, created and updated time) is written with its change (DD-031), and an existing record's created time stays. Any other error ends the patch file: its later patches are not applied, and the failing patch is not recorded MDL-07 Every action: a typeName that is not stored fails with PATCH_FOR_UNKNOWN_TYPE (action, type name). A patch applies when the type's typeVersion is absent, equals applyToVersion ignoring case, or starts with applyToVersion followed by .; otherwise it is SKIPPED. An applied patch sets typeVersion to updateToVersion and stores the type with TDS-07 and TDS-08. An action given a kind it does not handle fails with PATCH_NOT_APPLICABLE_FOR_TYPE (action, Java class name such as AtlasEnumDef) MDL-08 UPDATE_ENUMDEF (enums): adds each of elementDefs, replacing an element with the same value MDL-09 ADD_ATTRIBUTE (entities, classifications, structs, relationships) and UPDATE_ATTRIBUTE (entities, classifications, structs): add each of attributeDefs at the end, replacing an attribute with the same name. TDS-08 applies, so a changed attribute type or a new mandatory attribute fails MDL-10 ADD_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE (entities, classifications, structs): of attributeDefs, keeps those the type does not have that are mandatory, have a non-empty default value, have a primitive type and are not unique; an unknown attribute type fails with its registry error. With none kept the patch is SKIPPED; otherwise they are added, and the update may add mandatory attributes MDL-11 REMOVE_LEGACY_REF_ATTRIBUTES (relationships; any other kind ends UNKNOWN): the label is params.relationshipLabel, else __ and the qualified name of the attribute at the one legacy end, else the current label; with both ends legacy and no label it fails with PATCH_MISSING_RELATIONSHIP_LABEL. The ends swap when params.swapEnds is true, params.relationshipCategory replaces the category, and the attribute each end names is removed from its entity type. The relationship and both entity types are one update, in which attributes may be removed, the category may change and the ends may swap MDL-12 UPDATE_TYPEDEF_OPTIONS (any kind): fails with PATCH_INVALID_DATA without typeDefOptions, before the version check; merges them into the options, the patch's winning. SET_SERVICE_TYPE (any kind): sets the serviceType; without one the stored one stays, as TDS-07 keeps a blank serviceType MDL-13 UPDATE_ATTRIBUTE_METADATA (entities, structs): to the attributes named attributeName, ignoring case, applies each of params: searchWeight, a number, -1 or 1 to 10; indexType, DEFAULT or STRING, ignored when empty. Any other parameter or value is an error that ends the patch file (MDL-06). A type without the attribute still has the patch APPLIED MDL-14 ADD_SUPER_TYPES (entities): without superTypes the patch is SKIPPED, before the version check; otherwise each is added MDL-15 Each model file and each patch is one change of the typedef store (TDS-10, TDS-11), decided on the newest stored definitions and records: when another process wrote first, it is decided again, so processes starting together create, update and patch each type once (DD-033) MDL-16 The server loads the models after the stored definitions (TDS-12) and before it answers, from AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_MODELS_DIR, by default the vendored 2.4.0 models, which are byte-identical to addons/models of release-2.4.0. Built-in model types and patch records name no user (DV-07)

items.title: 6.1 Authentication
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: #91, extended onto 0.6
  • Records: DD-036 to DD-040; DV-10, DV-11, DV-12 (DV-04 and DV-06 are retired when this lands); relies on ADR 007, ADR 039, ADR 046, ADR 052, DD-034

items.title: Scope
items.text:
The server becomes an OpenID Connect relying party in front of the shared identity provider (dev/keycloak, ADR 007), the dashboards learn who the user is, and every endpoint except the few Java Atlas keeps public starts demanding a principal. This ports the Keycloak mode of Atlas 2.4.0 (atlas.authentication.method.keycloak on): the adapter's browser flow, its session, its bearer acceptance, its CSRF filter, and the session endpoint's user and groups.

  • apps/aurelius-atlas-server: a new auth module — OIDC discovery and JWKS verification, the authorization-code flow, server-side sessions with the ATLASSESSIONID cookie, bearer access-token verification, the AtlasCSRFPreventionFilter port, and the guard that admits or rejects every request; admin/session reports the real user and groups.
  • dev/keycloak: a confidential client for the Atlas relying party, realm roles for the dev users, in import/master.json.
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-dashboard: nginx gates page loads with auth_request and hands unauthenticated browsers to the server's login start (DD-036); the resolved config and its shipped template change together. No vendored dashboard source changes (ADR 046).

Not in scope:

Not delivered here Delivered by Per-endpoint authorization policies (who may read/write what) 6.2 (simple authorizer only, DV-02) File/LDAP/PAM/Knox login not planned (ADR 050) createdBy/updatedBy on type definitions and audit 1.4–1.5 retro-fit; DV-06 retired here Saved searches per user 4.5 (UserProfileService) Shared session state across server replicas not planned (HA not planned) TLS and issuer changes none; issuer is keycloak.localhost

items.title: Semantics
items.text: Configuration names follow the FastAPI example's pattern; all are AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_-prefixed (SRV-01). The relying-party registration mirrors the adapter config of AtlasSecurityConfig#adapterDeploymentContext (atlas.authentication.method.keycloak.{realm,auth-server-url,resource,credentials-secret}).

items.title: The guard
items.text: Id Rule AUTH-01 Authentication is on when an issuer is configured; with no issuer configured the server answers as before and the session reports no user (DV-04, scoped to unconfigured installations) AUTH-02 Every Atlas API request needs a valid principal, except admin/status, admin/liveness and admin/readiness (DV-12) and the auth endpoints themselves (/api/atlas/auth/*, /logout.html); static files are served by the dashboard origin and are never guarded (DSH-08) AUTH-03 A request carrying Authorization: Bearer <token> is authenticated by verifying the token against the issuer's JWKS (signature, iss, aud, exp); it never creates or touches a session; an invalid bearer is answered 401 AUTH-04 An unauthenticated API request is answered 401 with the Atlas error body (SRV-04), never with a redirect — an expired session mid-use looks like an error to the dashboard, which has a 401 handler (DV-11) AUTH-05 A CSRF-protected browser request (CRS-01) without a valid session fails the CSRF check — there is no token to match — and is answered as CRS-01 dictates, before the endpoint or any redirect logic is reached

items.title: The browser flow and the session
items.text: Id Rule AUTH-06 GET /api/atlas/auth/login, reached for a guarded page load without a valid session (DSH-07), 302s to the issuer's authorization endpoint (authorization-code flow with PKCE, state and nonce kept server-side) with the registered redirect URI; the intended URL is kept and returned to after login AUTH-07 GET /api/atlas/auth/callback exchanges the code, validates the id_token (JWKS signature, iss, nonce, expiry — the login belongs to this flow) and the access_token (signature, iss, aud, expiry), creates the session from the access token's claims (DD-038 — Keycloak keeps roles out of the id_token, as AtlasKeycloakAuthenticationProvider reads the access token), and 302s to the kept URL; a state mismatch or a failed exchange is answered 401 and creates no session AUTH-08 The session cookie is ATLASSESSIONID — HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax; the session id is minted at login and never accepted from the query string (no URL rewriting); the server keeps sessions in memory (in-process) AUTH-09 The server refreshes the session's access token with the stored refresh token before it expires; when the refresh fails, the session is destroyed and requests to it are answered as unauthenticated (AUTH-04 for the API, AUTH-06 for a page load) AUTH-10 GET or POST /logout.html at the origin destroys the session, expires the cookie, and sends the browser to the issuer's end-session endpoint, with /login.jsp as the post-logout redirect — Atlas's logoutSuccessUrl — and landing back at it, where the login page answers and the login flow starts again (DV-10, DD-040)

items.title: The session endpoint
items.text: Id Rule ADM-06 With authentication on, GET /api/atlas/admin/session on a valid session or bearer reports userName (the token's preferred username) and groups (the union of the user's realm roles and the relying-party client's roles, deduplicated, first-seen order); the other session values keep their server-wide defaults, and both entity permissions stay false until the authorizer arrives (6.2) ADM-07 When a session idle timeout is configured, the session response carries atlas.session.timeout.secs so the dashboard's idle timer matches it; an idle session is destroyed and answers as unauthenticated

items.title: CSRF
items.text: Id Rule CRS-01 A request whose User-Agent matches the browser regex (^Mozilla.*,^Opera.*,^Chrome) and whose method is not in atlas.rest-csrf.methods-to-ignore (default GET,OPTIONS,HEAD,TRACE) must carry the custom header (X-XSRF-HEADER by default) with the session's CSRF token; a missing or wrong header is answered 400 with the JSON body {"msgDesc": "Missing header or invalid Header value for CSRF Vulnerability Protection"}, as in Atlas CRS-02 The _csrfToken the session reports is minted at the first session call on the session (20 letters and digits, ADM-05's form) and stays the same for the session's whole life CRS-03 A request whose User-Agent does not match the browser regex is exempt from the CSRF check — the path service clients (and bearer calls without a browser UA) take, as in Atlas

items.title: The dashboard origin
items.text: Id Rule DSH-07 An unauthenticated browser request for a dashboard page (/, /index.html, /n, /n/) is redirected to the server's login start and, after Keycloak, back to the intended page; an authenticated page load is served unchanged DSH-08 Static assets (JS, CSS, images, favicons) are served without authentication, as in Atlas's ignore list, so the login flow's own assets load DSH-09 /login.jsp — Atlas's login URI (AtlasLoginServlet), its logoutSuccessUrl, and the vendored UI's 401 landing — is the fifth gated page: an anonymous visit takes the login start with the URI kept (as Atlas's adapter runs the dance through it), and a visit on a session is served the login page, which resolves to the dashboard the user was on: the session's atlas.ui.default.version picks the default, the browser's last_ui_load wins over it, and a URL fragment carries over — the resolver of Atlas's login form (DD-040)

items.title: The parity harness with authentication on
items.text:
Id Rule SCN-16 A scenario may declare needs_auth: true: a harness that runs a guard-on installation passes it (load_scenarios(..., authenticated_run=True)), and a plain run skips it with the reason — its expectations exist only where the guard answers (AUTH-01's guard-off installation reports no user)

DD-036 explains why page-load gating lives in nginx while the OIDC flow lives in the server; DD-037 fixes the server as the relying party and keeps the OIDC plumbing inside aurelius_atlas_server until the template's example retires (DD-019).

items.title: Java origin
items.text:
Apache Atlas release-2.4.0:

  • server-common/.../security/AtlasKeycloakAuthenticationProvider.java: token → principal, role → authority extraction (what groups reports)
  • webapp/.../web/security/AtlasSecurityConfig.java: the Keycloak filter chain, the KeycloakAuthenticationEntryPoint browser redirect, the public ignore list (/login.jsp kept guarded under Keycloak), SessionCreationPolicy.ALWAYS, session-fixation newSession, logout at /logout.html with KeycloakLogoutHandler, logoutSuccessUrl("/login.jsp") and deleteCookies("ATLASSESSIONID") (DD-040), and the adapter config keys
  • webapp/src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/web.xml, AtlasLoginServlet, login.html.template, dashboardv2/public/js/modules/atlasLogin.js: /login.jsp as the login page and the last_ui_load resolver DSH-09 repeats
  • webapp/.../web/filters/AtlasCSRFPreventionFilter.java: CRS-01 to CRS-03 and ATLAS-401-00-040
  • webapp/.../web/resources/AdminResource.java#getUserProfile: user and groups in the session response
  • dashboardv2/public/js/main.js, utils/CommonViewFunction.js, views/site/Header.js: the origin contract this must satisfy — the session fetch before start-up, the 401/403 handler, the idle timer reading atlas.session.timeout.secs, and the logout link to /logout.html

items.title: Deviations
items.text:
Added to Deviations with this increment:

  • DV-10: the browser dance is nginx auth_request plus the server's login start under /api/ rather than the adapter's /login.jsp URI, because the dashboards are served by a separate process (DD-034) and the vendored UI is not touched (ADR 046).
  • DV-11: an expired session hits by XHR is answered 401 with the Atlas error body where Atlas's entry point redirects the browser to Keycloak and the XHR receives its login page as HTML.
  • DV-12: admin/liveness and admin/readiness stay unauthenticated; container probes and load balancers cannot hold a session. (admin/status is public in Atlas too.)
  • DV-13: the session's atlas.entity.update.allowed and atlas.entity.create.allowed report false: the authorizer that answers them per user is increment 6.2, so 6.1 reports the user without yet reporting what the user may do.

Retired when this increment lands: DV-04 (authentication exists; its open behaviour survives only for unconfigured installations, AUTH-01) and DV-06 (the server knows a user).

items.title: Acceptance
items.text:
• apps/aurelius-atlas-server/scenarios/admin/session.scenario.yaml — gains the authenticated variant (ADM-06, the Java example userName: admin, groups: [ADMIN] met by a dev user holding the ADMIN realm role) and the DV-04 deviation rows are removed.
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-server/tests/ — the guard (AUTH-01 to AUTH-05) against a Keycloak testcontainer (the pattern of the FastAPI example's auth tests), bearer verification, session and refresh (AUTH-06 to AUTH-10), CSRF (CRS-01 to CRS-03), session user and groups (ADM-06, ADM-07); every function named by a @pytest.mark.covers(..., rules=[...]) marker (ADR 049).
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-server/e2e/ — the stack grows dev/keycloak; tests log in as aurelius-writer (gets ADMIN) and aurelius-reader (no roles) and prove the flow over TLS.
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-dashboard/e2e/ — DSH-07 to DSH-09 with Playwright: an unauthenticated load lands on Keycloak's login and back; signing out of dashboardv3 and back in returns to it (DD-040); assets load without a session; the header shows the logged-in user (conftest starts Keycloak with the stack).
  • Run: uv run pytest apps/aurelius-atlas-server/tests, nx test aurelius-atlas-server -c ci, nx e2e aurelius-atlas-server -c ci, nx e2e aurelius-atlas-dashboard -c ci, and uv run aurelius-atlas-trace check for the gaps.

items.title: Specification Template
items.text:
Copy the block below into N-M-short-slug.md and fill it in before writing code.

# N.M Increment title

- **Status:** planned | in progress | in review | done
- **Pull request:** link
- **Records:** ADR / DD numbers this increment adds or relies on

## Scope

What this increment delivers: endpoints, operations, projects. Then what it explicitly does not
deliver, with the increment that will.

## Semantics

Each rule the behaviour must obey, in plain words, with an id that tests name in
`@pytest.mark.covers(..., rules=["XXX-NN"])`.

| Id     | Rule |
| ------ | ---- |
| XXX-01 |      |

## Java origin

The Atlas classes (2.4.0) whose behaviour this ports, so reviewers can compare.

## Deviations

Deliberate differences from Apache Atlas, each added to [Deviations](../deviations.md).

## Acceptance

The parity scenarios and test files that prove the rules, and how to run them.

items.title: Change Management
items.text:
The change management process ensures that features and fixes are developed, tested, and released in a controlled and efficient manner. It follows a structured flow from development through testing to a release, and hands the released version to the environments a project or customer operates.

The environments the system itself operates are two: development, which is each person's own machine, and test, which is the pipeline. Acceptance and production are not operated by the system; they exist per engagement, and the release hands over an artifact complete enough for a deployment to promote from. The reasoning behind that split is recorded in ADR 024.

items.title: Development
items.text:
During the development phase, developers work on new features or fixes in their local development environments. Each developer has their own isolated environment, which allows them to work independently without affecting others. The development environment is set up as a development container, which includes all necessary tools and dependencies, and runs the whole system — the application and the infrastructure it depends on — on the developer's machine.

Developers commit their changes to a feature branch in the GitHub repository. This branch is created from the main branch and is used to isolate the changes until they are ready for review and testing.

items.title: Test
items.text:
The testing phase is where the new functionality is validated before it is merged into the main branch. This phase is crucial for maintaining code quality and ensuring that new features do not introduce bugs or regressions.

Testing takes place in the test environment: the GitHub Actions pipeline. This environment runs automated checks and tests to ensure that the code meets the project's quality standards.

The following types of testing are performed:

  • Code Quality: Code is checked for formatting, linting, and other quality metrics.
  • Unit Testing: Tests individual units of code in isolation to ensure they work correctly.
  • Integration Testing: Tests the interaction between different units of code to ensure they work together.
  • End-to-End Testing: Tests the entire system against real services, not substitutes.

When the automated tests pass, the feature branch is ready for peer review. Another developer reviews the code changes, provides feedback, and approves the pull request. Once approved, the changes are merged into the main branch.

items.title: Release
items.text: A version of the system is released as one versioned whole: one number, one changelog, and one release event that publishes every deployable part together as signed, provenance-bearing artifacts. Passing the test environment is what qualifies a change to be part of a release.

items.title: Acceptance and Production
items.text:
What happens to a released version beyond the pipeline is decided per project or customer, because acceptance and production are where an engagement's own requirements live — who signs off, on what environment, under what schedule. The system's obligation to those environments is the hand-over: a released artifact that is signed, versioned, and configured only through the settings the environment supplies, so a deployment can promote it, and roll it back, without knowledge that lives only with the people who built it.

A project that wants promotion to acceptance and production to be a declared, repeatable path writes that path against the released artifacts, as part of its own deployment arrangement.

items.title: Testing Strategy
items.text: This document defines how testing is planned, executed, and maintained across the workspace.

items.title: Goals
items.text: The testing strategy exists to protect customer value while improving delivery throughput.

items.title: Protect customer trust
items.text:
Testing protects customer trust by reducing defects in critical workflows, lowering incidents related to reliability, security, and data integrity, and increasing confidence in every production release. This includes preventing:

  • Data corruption through validation of business logic and database operations
  • Security vulnerabilities via authentication/authorization testing and input sanitization checks
  • Service outages by validating system resilience and error handling
  • Regulatory non-compliance through audit trail verification and data governance tests

items.title: Improve delivery predictability
items.text: Testing improves delivery predictability by catching regressions early, establishing clear quality gates for pull requests and release candidates, and supporting a consistent release cadence across teams.

items.title: Reduce cost of change
items.text: Testing reduces the cost of change by surfacing issues earlier—during development rather than production—when fixes are faster and less expensive. This lowers rework from escaped defects and shortens investigation time through reliable, repeatable feedback.

items.title: Enable developer productivity
items.text: Testing enables developer productivity by reducing cognitive load for contributors, providing fast local feedback loops, and minimizing friction in the development workflow. Well-structured tests serve as living documentation that clarifies expected behavior and reduces the time spent understanding system functionality.

items.title: Enable scalable team execution
items.text: Testing enables scalable team execution by standardizing expectations across projects, making onboarding easier through clear conventions, and supporting parallel development with confidence in integration boundaries.

items.title: Metrics and indicators
items.text:
The testing strategy should improve the following indicators over time.

Business-aligned quality

Test coverage is a means, not the end goal. The primary objective is reliable business outcomes: stable releases, fewer incidents, and faster delivery.

items.title: Key performance indicators
items.text:
Indicator Desired direction Example target Business intent Change failure rate (CFR) Down < 15% Reduce release risk and increase confidence in delivery. Mean time to restore (MTTR) Down < 1 hour Reduce customer and operational impact when failures occur. Lead time for changes Down < 7 days Improve speed and predictability of delivery from start of development to production.

About the indicators

The above indicators are based on the DORA metrics, which are widely recognized as key measures of software delivery performance.

Example targets are provided as starting points. Actual targets should be operationalized in the context of team goals together with business stakeholders during implementation.

Measurement methodology
  • Change failure rate: Calculated from deployment logs and incident tracking systems (e.g., failed deployments / total deployments)
  • Mean time to restore: Measured from incident detection to service restoration, tracked in the incident management system
  • Lead time for changes: Tracked from commit to production deployment using CI/CD pipeline metadata

items.title: Supporting leading indicators
items.text:
Leading indicators provide early warning signals before customer-facing impact:

Indicator Desired direction Purpose Pull request quality gate pass rates Upward / stable Early detection of integration issues Flaky test rate Downward Maintain CI reliability and trust Mean time to fix flaky tests Downward Reduce test debt and improve feedback speed Recurring regression incidents Downward Improve test coverage for previously failing scenarios Test execution time (unit layer) Stable / downward Ensure fast local feedback loops Test execution time (integration layer) Stable / downward Maintain CI pipeline efficiency Coverage of critical business paths Upward Prioritize testing on high-value functionality Percentage of changes with test updates Upward Maintain confidence as the codebase evolves

items.title: Approach
items.text:
The strategy supports these goals through consistent patterns and tooling that provide fast local feedback for contributors, reliable validation of cross-service behavior, and predictable CI execution for pull requests and releases.

To achieve this, our testing model follows a testing pyramid:

  • Unit tests: high volume, fast execution, isolated behavior
  • Integration tests: medium volume, service boundaries, realistic dependencies
  • End-to-end (E2E) tests: focused volume, critical user and data workflows

items.title: Unit tests
items.text:
Unit tests validate individual functions, classes, and modules in isolation.

Use unit tests to verify business logic quickly, lock in behavior for edge cases and regressions, and refactor safely with immediate feedback. Unit tests should be deterministic and independent, run in milliseconds to low seconds, and avoid real network or infrastructure dependencies.

items.title: Integration tests
items.text:
Integration tests validate interactions between components and external systems.

Use integration tests to confirm API to database behavior, validate messaging flows and service contracts, and verify configuration and startup assumptions. These tests should run against realistic, typically containerized, infrastructure with explicit setup and teardown boundaries and focused assertions at integration points.

Contract testing

For microservice architectures, consider adding contract testing as an extension of integration tests to validate:

  • API schema compatibility between services
  • Message format consistency across service boundaries
  • Backward compatibility guarantees during version changes

items.title: End-to-end (E2E) tests
items.text:
E2E tests validate complete workflows across system boundaries.

Use E2E tests to verify user-critical paths from entry to outcome, validate end-to-end data consistency, and confirm deployment-like behavior before release. Compared to unit and integration tests, E2E suites should remain smaller due to higher runtime cost, with strong emphasis on reliability and low flake rate.

items.title: Python
items.text:
Unit and integration tests use pytest.

Recommended pytest plugins
  • pytest-cov - Coverage reporting
  • pytest-xdist - Parallel test execution
  • pytest-mock - Mocking support
Test naming convention

Test files should be named test\_\_\*.py (e.g., test__entity_producer.py). Test functions should follow the pattern test__<function_name>_<scenario> for unit tests and test__<function_name>_<scenario>_<expected_outcome> for integration tests to clarify intent and expected results.

Fixture best practices
  • Use function-scoped fixtures (@pytest.fixture()) for mutable state
  • Use session-scoped fixtures only for expensive shared infrastructure (e.g., database connections, containerized services)
  • Prefer parametrized fixtures for testing multiple scenarios without duplication
Parametrized tests

Use @pytest.mark.parametrize to test multiple input and expected output combinations without duplicating test code:

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "input_value,expected_output",
    [
        ("valid", "result1"),
        ("invalid", "error"),
    ],
)
def test_function(input_value, expected_output): ...

items.title: Angular
items.text:
Unit tests use Jest or Vitest. Choose Jest for broader ecosystem support and Vitest for faster execution in Vite-based projects.

File naming convention

Test files should be named *.spec.ts (e.g., entity-producer.service.spec.ts) and placed alongside the implementation file for easy navigation.

Describe block organization

Organize related behavior with describe blocks, limiting nesting to a maximum of 3 levels for readability:

describe("UserService", () => {
    describe("when authenticated", () => {
        describe("#getUser", () => {
            it("should return user data", () => { ... });
        });
    });
});
Behavior naming convention

Use should <condition> when <scenario> pattern:

  • should display error message when form is invalid
  • should navigate to dashboard after successful login
Mocking best practices
  • Use shallow mocks for service dependencies (mock only the methods being tested)
  • Use deep mocks sparingly, as they can hide integration issues
  • Isolate HTTP behavior using test-time mocks via HttpClientTestingModule

items.title: Java
items.text:
Unit tests use JUnit 5.

File naming convention

Test files should be named *Test.java (e.g., EntityProducerTest.java). Package structure should mirror the main codebase for easy navigation (e.g., src/test/java/com/aurelius/producer/).

Assertion style

Prefer AssertJ for fluent assertions over built-in JUnit assertions or Hamcrest:

assertThat(entity.getName()).isEqualTo("Test Entity");
assertThatThrownBy(() -> entity.setGuid(null))
    .isInstanceOf(NullPointerException.class);
Mockito usage

Use Mockito for isolation and interaction verification:

  • @Mock for creating mock dependencies
  • @InjectMocks for injecting mocks into the test subject
  • verify() for interaction verification
Test isolation patterns
  • Use @BeforeEach to set up fresh state for each test
  • Use @AfterEach to clean up any modifications made during tests
  • Avoid static mutable state that can cause test interference
Parameterized tests

Use @ParameterizedTest with various sources:

@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(strings = { "valid", "also-valid" })
void testValidation(String input) {
    assertThat(isValid(input)).isTrue();
}

items.title: Testcontainers
items.text:
For integration and end-to-end testing, use Testcontainers as the default approach for provisioning dependent services.

Benefits of Testcontainers

Prefer ephemeral, containerized dependencies over shared static environments for integration tests. This provides:

  • Isolation: Each test gets a fresh environment, reducing flakiness from shared state.
  • Realism: Tests run against actual service images, improving confidence in production-like behavior.
  • Flexibility: Easily configure different versions and setups for testing various scenarios.
Validating containerized applications

Consider running containerized applications in a Testcontainers-managed container during testing. This provides higher confidence that the tested behavior matches production-like conditions, including configuration, environment variables, and network interactions.

Multi-service scenarios with Docker Compose

Use DockerCompose from testcontainers.compose when multiple services are required.

from pathlib import Path
from testcontainers.compose import DockerCompose


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def compose() -> Generator[DockerCompose]:
    """Return a Docker Compose instance."""
    context = Path(__file__).parent.absolute()
    with DockerCompose(context=context, env_file=dotenv.find_dotenv()) as compose:
        yield compose
Wait strategies

Use appropriate wait strategies for common services. The codebase uses HealthcheckWaitStrategy for services with health checks defined in Docker Compose.

from pathlib import Path
from testcontainers.compose import DockerCompose


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def compose() -> Generator[DockerCompose]:
    """Return a Docker Compose instance."""
    context = Path(__file__).parent.absolute()
    with DockerCompose(context=context, env_file=dotenv.find_dotenv()) as compose:
        yield compose.waiting_for(
            {
                "aurelius-atlas-fastapi-example": HealthcheckWaitStrategy(),
            },
        )
Service discovery

Use get_service_host_and_port() or get_service_port() to retrieve runtime connection details:

hostname, port = compose.get_service_host_and_port("postgres-app", settings.database_port)

if not (hostname and port):
    raise ValueError("PostgreSQL service not found in Docker Compose")
Log capture

Containers are automatically torn down when exiting the context manager. The capture_docker_compose_logs() helper ensures logs are captured for debugging:

from aurelius_atlas_sdk.testing.testcontainers import capture_docker_compose_logs

with DockerCompose(context=context) as compose:
    yield compose.waiting_for({"service": HealthcheckWaitStrategy()})
    capture_docker_compose_logs(compose)

items.title: Playwright
items.text:
For frontend end-to-end testing, use Playwright to validate functional behavior and critical user flows. The codebase uses Playwright with pytest integration via playwright.sync_api.

Basic assertion

Use Playwright's built-in assertions for common checks:

from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect


def test_main_page_has_welcome_message(authenticated: Page) -> None:
    expect(authenticated.get_by_text(re.compile("Welcome"))).to_be_visible()
Authentication fixture

The codebase uses pytest fixtures to handle authentication before tests run. A typical authenticated fixture navigates to the app and performs Keycloak login:

@pytest.fixture()
def authenticated(page: Page, base_url: str, settings: Settings) -> Page:
    """Authenticate the user and return the page."""
    page.goto(base_url)

    # Navigate to Keycloak login
    page.wait_for_url(re.compile(f"/realms/{settings.auth_realm_name}/protocol/openid-connect/auth"))

    # Fill credentials and sign in
    page.locator("#username").fill(settings.username)
    page.locator("#password").fill(settings.password.get_secret_value())
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()

    # Wait for redirect back to app
    page.wait_for_url(re.compile(base_url))

    return page
Locator patterns

Use semantic locators (test IDs, labels, roles) for more resilient tests:

  • page.locator("#search-input") - ID-based locator
  • page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in") - ARIA role-based locator
  • page.get_by_text(re.compile("Welcome")) - Text-based locator with regex
Assertions

Common assertion patterns used in the codebase:

# Visibility check
expect(search_input).to_be_visible()

# Attribute check
expect(search_input).to_have_attribute("placeholder", "Search for an entity")

# Count check
expect(authenticated.locator(".search-result-card")).to_have_count(len(entities))

# Text content check
expect(authenticated.get_by_text(re.compile(f"I have found {len(entities)} entities\\."))).to_be_visible()
Test isolation

Each test should receive a fresh Page instance through the fixture, ensuring tests don't interfere with each other. The authenticated fixture handles login state separately from individual test logic.

items.title: Chromatic
items.text: For visual testing of UI components, use Chromatic to catch regressions in shared UI components and maintain visual consistency. The visual review workflow also allows for non-technical stakeholders to triage and approve visual changes.

items.title: Review workflow
items.text:
Define who approves visual changes based on component type:

  • Design system components: Require designer approval
  • Feature components: Developer approval sufficient for non-breaking changes
  • Layout changes: PM and designer review required

items.title: Integration with Storybook
items.text:
Chromatic integrates directly with Storybook to automatically capture component states. Ensure all stories are documented and represent actual usage patterns in the application.

Best practices reinforcement

The Chromatic visual testing workflow together with Storybook reinforces best practices around component isolation and documentation in the project.

items.title: Naming and organization conventions
items.text:
Language Test file pattern Test function pattern Python test\_\_\*.py test\_\_<function_name>_<scenario> Angular \*.spec.ts should <behavior> when <condition> Java \*Test.java test<Method>_<scenario>_<outcome>

General organization rules:

  1. Keep tests independent and order-agnostic.
  2. Use behavior-oriented names that describe intent.
  3. Follow Arrange, Act, Assert (AAA) structure.
  4. Prefer reusable fixtures/builders over copy-pasted setup.

items.title: Test data and environment management
items.text:
Quality and stability depend on disciplined environment control.

Use environment variables and typed settings for configuration, create test data through fixtures or factories rather than manual shared state, clean up generated data after each test or fixture scope, and avoid hidden dependencies between test modules.

Fixture scopes

Use session-scoped fixtures only for expensive shared infrastructure. Use function-scoped fixtures for mutable state.

items.title: CI/CD integration
items.text: Testing is orchestrated with Nx and executed in GitHub Actions.

items.title: Nx integration
items.text: Nx provides task orchestration across projects, affected-project execution for efficient pull request validation, task caching to reduce repeated work, and parallel execution for independent tasks.

items.title: Core commands
items.text:
Use these commands during development and CI troubleshooting:

# Test one project
nx test <project-name>

# Run E2E for one project
nx e2e <project-name>

# Test affected projects
nx affected -t test e2e -c ci

# Run test target across many projects
nx run-many -t test

items.title: CI pipeline expectations
items.text:
CI validation includes:

  1. Runtime and dependency setup (Java, Python, Node.js)
  2. Lint/format and pre-commit quality gates
  3. Affected test and E2E execution
  4. Browser setup for frontend E2E
  5. Visual regression checks where configured

Merge criteria

Pull requests are expected to pass all required affected test stages before merge.

items.title: Flaky test management
items.text:
When a test is flaky, follow this sequence:

  1. Identify recurring failure patterns in CI.
  2. Investigate root causes (timing, isolation, environment).
  3. Fix underlying issues before considering retries.
  4. Document known flake status and ownership.

items.title: Ongoing maintenance
items.text: Maintain test quality by reviewing coverage trends regularly, removing redundant or low-value tests, refactoring duplicated setup logic, and updating tests as contracts and dependencies evolve.

items.title: Contributor checklist
items.text:
Before opening a pull request, confirm that:

  • New behavior is covered at the correct test layer
  • Existing tests were updated for changed contracts
  • Affected project tests pass locally
  • Any new infrastructure requirements are documented.

items.title: Data Encryption
items.text: This page answers where data is encrypted, from the data-protection record (ADR 039). Whether a path is protected is answered from configuration, not by probing a running system (R5) — this page names where the configuration lives.

items.title: In transit
items.text:
Every path data travels on inside the system is TLS with certificate verification against a local certificate authority:

Path Mechanism Browser → nginx / FastAPI TLS (ssl_certificate in the nginx config, uvicorn ssl_certfile); the dev-server proxy and E2E verify (browser page loads: named relaxation below). Service → PostgreSQL sslmode=verify-full + CA bundle; server ssl=on with TLS-only client authentication. Service → Kafka / Schema Registry TLS listeners only: apps use SASL_SSL (OAuth bearer tokens, ADR 013), infrastructure links use SSL (mTLS); registry and Connect serve HTTPS; clients pass the CA (or JVM truststore) explicitly — also for the token-endpoint call to Keycloak. Service → OpenTelemetry collector OTLP over TLS (gRPC 4317 / HTTP 4318); exporters trust the CA. Service → Keycloak (token verify) HTTPS issuer with CA trust in CI/E2E; the local development browser path is the named relaxation below.

The PostgreSQL posture is tested, not just configured: unit-test containers (aurelius_atlas_sdk.testing.tls, via tls_certificates and configure_tls_postgres) start the same hardened image with ssl=on and a TLS-only client authentication file using an ephemeral per-run certificate authority, and connect with sslmode=verify-full — the same arrangement the dev and E2E services use.

items.title: At rest
items.text: Encryption at rest is owned by the stores and is not configured in this repository; deployments choose store-level encryption (disk or volume encryption). Development data is throwaway and carries no at-rest guarantee — the arrangement states this rather than implying it.

items.title: Named relaxation (development arrangement only)
items.text:
• Keycloak additionally serves a plaintext HTTP listener (port 8080) so the developer browser opens a familiar URL; its TLS listener (8443) serves every CI/E2E path.
  • Browser-facing developer surfaces (SPA dev-server, Grafana, Kafka UI, Node-RED, Storybook) stay plaintext on a developer machine.
  • Playwright's bundled browsers carry their own trust stores and cannot enroll the mkcert root, so frontend E2E page navigation skips browser certificate verification (ignore_https_errors). The E2E suite verifies the same browser-facing endpoint against the CA out-of-band (hostname + chain), and nginx still verifies the backend with proxy_ssl_verify.

CI and E2E run all of these paths over TLS and verify certificates, except the browser navigation relaxation above. Each plaintext occurrence in this repository carries a comment naming ADR 039.

items.title: Certificates
items.text: Each project that serves or consumes TLS owns a tls.json listing the certificates it needs; nx certgen issues them from an mkcert local CA into the project's own gitignored certs/ directory — PEM keypairs, PKCS12 keystores, a JVM truststore.p12 where needed, and a ca.pem copy for pure clients. The CA itself has no workspace home: certgen installs mkcert's own root CA into the system trust stores (it lives in mkcert's store, outside the repository) and copies it into each project's certs/. Generation is on demand: serve and e2e targets declare a certgen dependency, which also depends on decrypt because truststore passwords live encrypted in each project's .env.enc. Per-project certclean removes a project's material but never the CA; mkcert -uninstall drops the CA and its system trust entries entirely. They are development material only — a deployment replaces the CA and key material with its own.

items.title: Identity Management
items.text: This page answers how a person is admitted to Aurelius Atlas and where that lives, from the identity record (ADR 007). The authoritative rule set is the increment spec 6.1 Authentication; this page is the narrative and the diagrams, and cites rule ids (AUTH-*, CRS-*, DSH-*) rather than restating them.

items.title: One provider, one relying party
items.text:
Aurelius Atlas holds no user accounts and implements no sign-in page of its own. Keycloak is the only place people exist (ADR 007), and aurelius-atlas-server is its OpenID Connect relying party: it starts the browser flow, exchanges the code, verifies the tokens the provider issued, and keeps a session for the person the provider admitted. The server decides who a request is from; what that person may do is the authorizer's question (increment 6.2, DV-13).

The whole flow runs on the dashboard origin (https://localhost:8444 in dev). The session cookie and the dashboards' relative URLs need one origin, so the dashboard image serves the pages, gates them, and proxies /api/ to the server on the same origin (DD-034 in the design log, DV-09); the OIDC flow itself lives in the server (DD-036). nginx only asks the server whether a request has a session and redirects — it holds no token or session logic.

items.title: The guard
items.text:
Every request reaches one middleware in a fixed order (aurelius_atlas_server.auth.guard). Authentication is on when an issuer is configured (AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_AUTH_ISSUER); with no issuer the server answers as an open installation (AUTH-01, the retired DV-04's surviving case).

Step Decision Rule 1 Authentication off, or a public path (admin/status, admin/version, the liveness/readiness probes, /api/atlas/auth/*, /logout.html) — pass AUTH-01, AUTH-02, DV-12 2 The CSRF check for a browser User-Agent, before any authorisation CRS-01 3 A bearer token verifies against the issuer's JWKS and authenticates on its own, never touching a session AUTH-03 4 Otherwise the ATLASSESSIONID session, refreshed before its access token expires AUTH-08, AUTH-09 5 No principal: a navigation (Accept: text/html, not /api/) starts the login flow; an API call is answered 401 with the Atlas error body AUTH-04, AUTH-06, DV-11 
flowchart TD
    R[request] --> A{auth on?}
    A -- no --> P[pass through]
    A -- yes --> PUB{public path?}
    PUB -- yes --> P
    PUB -- no --> CSRF{CSRF ok?}
    CSRF -- no --> D4[400 CSRF body]
    CSRF -- yes --> B{bearer token?}
    B -- yes --> BV{verifies?}
    BV -- yes --> OK[Principal from token]
    BV -- no --> D5[401]
    B -- no --> S{session valid?}
    S -- yes --> OK2[Principal from session]
    S -- no --> W{navigation?}
    W -- yes --> L[302 login start, URL kept]
    W -- no --> D6[401 Atlas error body]

items.title: Signing in
items.text:
The dashboard's page load is the entry point. nginx asks the server /api/atlas/auth/check as an auth_request subrequest (the session cookie rides it) and, on a 401, redirects to the server's login start (error_page 401 = @login) with the intended page kept — never through an /api/… error_page path, which would re-enter the /api/ proxy (DD-036). The server runs the authorization-code flow with PKCE and returns to the kept URL.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant N as nginx (dashboard origin)
    participant S as aurelius-atlas-server
    participant K as Keycloak (issuer)
    B->>N: GET /n/ (page load)
    N->>S: auth_request /api/atlas/auth/check (cookie rides)
    S-->>N: 401 (no session)
    N-->>B: 302 /api/atlas/auth/login?next=/n/ (error_page lands in @login)
    B->>S: GET /api/atlas/auth/login?next=/n/ (proxied /api/)
    Note over S: keeps next=/n/ and mints state + nonce (AUTH-06)
    S-->>B: 302 authorize URL (PKCE, registered redirect_uri)
    B->>K: GET /protocol/openid-connect/auth?...
    K-->>B: login form (#kc-form-login)
    B->>K: username + password
    Note over K: signs an access token (realm roles) and an id_token (nonce)
    K-->>B: 302 callback?code=...&state=...
    B->>S: GET /api/atlas/auth/callback (AUTH-07)
    S->>K: POST token (code + PKCE verifier)
    K-->>S: access_token, id_token, refresh_token
    Note over S: verifies both, session minted from the ACCESS token claims (DD-038)
    S-->>B: 302 /n/ with Set-Cookie ATLASSESSIONID
    B->>N: GET /n/ again
    N->>S: auth_request /api/atlas/auth/check
    S-->>N: 200 (session)
    N-->>B: dashboardv3

The session's principal comes from the access token, not the id_token (DD-038): Keycloak keeps realm and client roles out of the id_token, and Atlas's own AtlasKeycloakAuthenticationProvider reads the access token too — which the token-exchange test asserts with a roleless id_token and a roled access token. GET /api/atlas/admin/session then reports userName and groups (the union of realm and client roles) to the dashboard (ADM-06).

items.title: Signing out, and back to the dashboard you left
items.text:
The two vendored dashboards record the UI a person is on in the browser's localStorage.last_ui_load (v3's header and 401 handler write "v2", v2's write "v1") and both navigate to the same /logout.html, so the server cannot tell the source UI from a request.
